 CSU faculty overwhelmingly authorize strike as contract negotiations remain unresolved
 In CSUSB NEWS 
 Nov 21, 2026
 By Stephen Day 
 Photography by Stephen Day 
 56 Views
 0 Comments 
 CSU faculty begin strike authorization vote as students face potential academic disruptions at CSUSB. 
 Stephen Day 
 CFA members made their voices heard as 97% vote to support strike authorization, CSUSB faculty prepare for possible labor action while students face uncertainty over classes, grades, and graduation.
 Faculty across the California State university system have overwhelmingly voted to authorize a strike, with 97% of voting California Faculty Association (CFA) members supporting a potential work stoppage as contract negotiations with CSU administration remain unresolved.
 The results, announced Nov. 20, give CFA leadership the authority to call a strike if the two sides can’t reach an agreement after completing the remaining steps of the bargaining process.
 No strike date has been announced, and faculty are not currently on strike.
 For students at CSUSB, the authorization brings the possibility of disrupted classes, delayed grades, and complications with graduation one step closer. CFA leadership says the vote demonstrates the willingness of faculty to take to the picket line, however, CSU administration maintains that an agreement remains possible and say contingency plans are in place to minimize disruption to students.
 Dr. Tiffany Jones, president of CFA’s San Bernardino chapter, described the vote as a clear message from faculty across the CSU system.
 “The 97% of faculty members who voted to support a strike authorization is a resoundingly clear statement,” Jones said in an email response to the Coyote Chronicle. “Faculty across the CSU, including us here at CSUSB, are united in saying that the current situation is not sustainable for us or for students.”
 Jones said CSUSB faculty participated in the vote in high numbers, but campus specific voting information is confidential.
 No one wants to disrupt the education of students, or take a pay cut to walk the picket lines, but this vote result shows just how serious faculty are.
 —  Dr. Tiffany Jones, CFA San Bernardino Chapter president 
 The union has been negotiating a new contract for approximately 20 months, seeking improvements in compensation, workload protections, lecturer job security, health care, academic freedom, and protections related to artificial intelligence.
 “Faculty, librarians, counsellors and coaches are resolved and are clearly stating that the CSU chancellor’s office needs to take our proposals seriously,” Jones said. 
CSU expresses disappointment, urges return to negotiations
 In a statement provided to the Coyote Chronicle following the authorization vote, CSU administration expressed disappointment with the results while emphasizing that a strike has not been called.
 “The California State University (CSU) respects the California Faculty Association’s (CFA) right to strike. However, we are disappointed by the outcome of the strike authorization vote,” the statement said.
 CSU pointed to five recently reached collective bargaining agreements covering more than 28,000 employees as evidence that negotiated settlements remain possible.
 “A strike authorization vote is a procedural step and does not mean a strike is imminent,” CSU said. “We believe the parties’ time and resources would be more productively spent at the bargaining table, where meaningful progress can be made, rather than preparing for a potential strike.”
 The university system also criticized the CFA’s decision to declare an impasse, arguing that it limited opportunities for continued negotiations.
 CSU said it has invited the CFA to resume direct negotiations in October but that the union did not accept the invitation.
 “As a result, CSU’s last proposal to the CFA did not have the opportunity to evolve through continued bargaining, as occurred with the five other unions,” the statement said.
 CFA has disputed CSU’s characterization of the invitation, arguing that the proposed discussions focused mostly on salary and failed to address outstanding demands involving workload, lecturer job security, health care, academic freedom, and artificial intelligence.
 In an earlier response to the Chronicle, CSU spokesperson Amy Bentley-Smith confirmed that campuses maintain contingency plans intended to minimize disruption to students academic progress.
 “The CSU and its universities maintain contingency plans for all types of potential disruptions to campus operations with the goal of preventing or reducing impact to our students’ academic progress,” Bentley-Smith said.
 However, CSU has not provided specific details about how a faculty strike might affect classes, grading, graduation, or financial aid.
 More than a dispute over salaries
 Unlike the previous CFA contract negotiations, which focused primarily on salary provisions, the current dispute involves broader collective bargaining agreement.
 In an October communication to members, CFA acknowledged that they received an invitation to resume negotiations but argued that the proposed discussions focused primarily on compensation.
 According to the CFA, the proposed salary framework included a one-time 5% bonus in place of a retroactive raise for the 2025-26, a 4% general salary increase upon ratification and another 4% increase in July 2027.
 The union argues that the proposal would not adequately address inflation and rising living costs, particularly because the one-time bonus would not permanently increase base salaires.
 The CFA has also criticized CSU administration’s spending priorities, including executive compensation decisions. In materials distributed to students, CFA-San Bernardino alleged that some campus presidents and vice chancellors have received raises of up to 20%.
 CSU has also committed $55 million for ChatGPT EDU access for faculty and students through 2029, despite strong pushback from students and faculty who argue that the investment prioritizes AI technology over human-led education.
 CSU emphasized the financial constraints facing the university system. In a previous statement to the Chronicle, Bentley-Smith said salaries and benefits accounted for 74% of CSU’s 2025-26 operating budget, including $4.3 billion in salaries and $2.3 billion in benefits.
 She also stated that faculty received general salary increases totaling 13% in recent bargaining rounds.
 Jones, however, argued that the dispute is about more than the compensation. She cited increasing class sizes, canceled courses, reduced funding for internships and independent studies, and faculty burnout as problems directly affecting students.
 “We’re not just fighting for us. We’re fighting for quality education, right? We’re fighting for the students,” Jones said.
 The union has also proposed contractual protections concerning artificial intelligence, including faculty intellectual property and professional judgment over how AI is used in teaching and other university work.
 The CFA argues that these issues can’t be resolved through salary increases alone.
 One student on Reddit amplified those concerns by saying “I’m not paying tuition to be taught by AI. I want to learn from REAL PEOPLE!!!”
 What should students do now
 Despite the strike authorization, Jones emphasized that students should continue their normal academic activities until an actual work stoppage is announced.
 “For now, my best advice for students is to keep attending classes and keep submitting work,” Jones said.
 She said the CFA would provide advance guidance about classes and other academic matters if a strike is called.
 CFA-San Bernardino has been distributing student information materials and working with Students for Quality Education (SQE), a student organization affiliated with the union, to raise awareness of the negotiations.
 The chapter has encouraged students to sign solidarity pledges, contact CSU leadership and state legislators, and participate in rallies, informational pickets, and other campus activities.
 Jones previously urged students not to cross faculty picket lines if a strike occurs, arguing that student solidarity could help bring the dispute to a faster resolution.
 “Short-term gain is not worth it for the long term. We want a better education system. We want better quality education,” Jones said.
 For students whose professors continue teaching during a strike, however, choosing to skip class could raise questions about attendance policies and academic consequences. CSU has not provided specific guidance on those circumstances would be handled.
 The CFA acknowledged the potential disruption while emphasizing its position that the union’s demands would ultimately benefit students.
 “You are not collateral in this dispute. You are the reason we do this work, and we will fight for you and keep you informed at every step,” the CFA San Bernardino chapter wrote.
 What happens now?
 Although the strike authorization has passed, CFA and CSU remain in the legally required factfinding process.
 The final factfinding hearing is scheduled for Dec. 10, a date Jones said was pushed back due to flight delays.
 After the hearing, the panel will prepare a report containing nonbinding recommendations for resolving the dispute. Once the report is issued, a 10-day confidential period will provide another opportunity for the parties to reach an agreement before the statutory process concludes.
 If no agreement is reached, the CFA could call a strike.
 For now, go to class, but remain informed by speaking with your professors and hearing their take on the why’s and how’s a strike might impact your classes. You can also follow the CFA on Instagram and the official CSUSB Instagram account .
 Information about local union activities and student resources is available through CFA-San Bernardino at their linktree , including a frequently asked questions page specifically for students.
 Stephen Day 
 Photo Editor
